summary: This document replaces some terminology in OSPF with wording in line with inclusive language used in the industry, following guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Future OSPF documents are meant to use the new terms, even when referring to the older RFCs it updates. It changes words, not protocol behavior.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some words in the OSPF rulebooks were swapped for kinder, clearer ones. The master and slave of a database exchange are now the Leader and the Follower, and the packet bit that marked the master is now the Leader bit.

Nothing about how OSPF works changes. The RFC lists which sentences and diagrams in seven earlier documents have to be reworded.

questions: what is the ospf leader bit
subtitle: Swaps the master/slave wording in OSPF for Leader/Follower across seven RFCs without changing how the protocol works.

tldr.problem: OSPF specifications described the database synchronization between two routers with the terms master and slave, and named a Database Description packet bit accordingly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces master/slave with Leader/Follower, renames the MS bit to the Leader (L) bit, and lists the sections of seven earlier RFCs affected. It also updates the IANA registry entry for the bit.
tldr.outcome: Only wording changes. OSPF operation and security characteristics are unchanged, and future OSPF documents are meant to use the new terms even when they reference the updated RFCs.

today: RFC 9454 was published in August 2023 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It amends RFC 2328, RFC 5340 and five other OSPF-related RFCs, and its terms are intended for all future OSPF documents.

sections.title: Why the Terms Changed
sections.content:
This document updates OSPF terminology to match the inclusive language used in the industry. The IETF has designated the US National Institute of Standards and Technology document "Guidance for NIST Staff on Using Inclusive Language in Documentary Standards", NISTIR 8366, as its inclusive language guideline.

It is intended that all future OSPF documents use the revised terminology, even when they reference the RFCs this document updates. The seven documents updated are RFC 2328, RFC 4222, RFC 4811, RFC 5243, RFC 5340, RFC 5614 and RFC 5838.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has adopted guidance on inclusive wording for its standards and applied it to the OSPF documents. This note lists which words change and in which books, so that everyone uses the same new words from now on.

sections.title: Leader and Follower in OSPFv2
sections.content:
The base OSPFv2 specification, RFC 2328, defines the synchronization of databases as two routers forming a master and slave relationship. All instances of these terms are replaced by Leader and Follower. In the Database Description packet, the master (MS) bit is renamed the Leader (L) bit.

The RFC states that the operation of OSPFv2 is not modified. The change reaches nine places in RFC 2328: "The Synchronization of Databases" in Section 7.2, "The Neighbor Data Structure" in Section 10, "Neighbor states" in Section 10.1, "Events causing neighbor state changes" in Section 10.2, "The Neighbor state machine" in Section 10.3, "Receiving Database Description Packets" in Section 10.6, "Sending Database Description Packets" in Section 10.8, "An Example" in Section 10.10, and "The Database Description packet" in Appendix A.3.3.

The same treatment is given to OSPFv3 in RFC 5340. That document defines the Database Description process between two routers as one being designated to be the master and the other the slave, and all instances of the terms are replaced by Leader and Follower. Its Master/Slave (MS) bit is renamed the Leader (L) bit. Here too the operation is unchanged, and the change reaches only "The Database Description Packet" in Appendix A.3.3.
sections.plainLanguage: When two routers compare their copies of the link-state database, one of them leads the exchange and the other follows. The names for those roles, and the name of the packet bit that marks the leading router, are what change. Every step of the exchange stays exactly as it was.

sections.title: The Other Documents That Change
sections.content:
Five more RFCs get smaller edits.

  • RFC 4222, a Best Current Practice document on prioritised treatment of OSPFv2 packets: in Appendix C, item 2, an example OSPFv2 packet sequence refers to the "slave" in a database exchange, and that reference becomes "Follower".
  • RFC 4811, Informational, on out-of-band link-state database resynchronization: in Section 2.4, which has a Database Description packet figure and a description of the encoding changes, every "MS" that refers to the packet bit becomes "L", and the reference to "Master" becomes "Leader".
  • RFC 5243, Informational, on database exchange summary list optimization: the Introduction, which refers to "Master or Slave", now refers to "Leader or Follower", and every instance of "Master" and "Slave" in the Section 3 example is renamed.
  • RFC 5614, Experimental, on a mobile ad hoc network extension of OSPF: in "Changes to the Neighbor State Machine" in Section 7.1, every "Master" and "Slave" becomes "Leader" and "Follower", and every "MS" that refers to the packet bit becomes "L". In "Receiving Database Description Packets" in Section 7.5, the parenthetical "master or slave" becomes "Leader or Follower".
  • RFC 5838, a Standards Track document on address families in OSPFv3: the Database Description packet figure in Section 2.7 has its "MS" field renamed to "L".

RFC 5838 also gets one rewritten paragraph. In the first paragraph of "Changes to the Hello Packet Processing" in Section 2.4, the text about a router that does not support the specification is rewritten so that it no longer uses the non-inclusive terms that referred to unreachability handling. The rewritten text explains that packets could be routed toward an interface and dropped because of misconfiguration or a software downgrade, and that a router which does not support the specification can still include such an interface in an SPF-calculated path as long as it establishes adjacencies using the Instance ID for the IPv4 address family, noting that OSPFv3 Router-LSAs and Network-LSAs are address-family agnostic.
sections.plainLanguage: Other OSPF documents mention the same old words in examples, diagrams and one longer explanation. Each one gets a list of the sentences to reword, and one paragraph in RFC 5838 is rewritten in full.

sections.title: The IANA Registry Update
sections.content:
IANA updated the "Database Description (DD) Packet Flags" registry. The description for value 0x01 is now "Leader (L-bit)", and the references are RFC 2328 and RFC 9454.

The flag keeps the same value and the same bit position. Only its name and description change, which matches the RFC's statement that protocol behaviour is untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of flag names got the new label, but the flag still sits in the same slot and does the same job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it updates terminology in OSPF RFCs without any modification to the specifications of the protocol. As a result, the security characteristics of OSPF do not change.

Implementers do not need to alter message processing, only the names used in documentation and, where applicable, in the registry entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Because only the names changed, nothing about how safe OSPF is has changed either.
